newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Populist Peters to play role of NZ kingmaker.
newsitem.headline: Populist Peters to play role of NZ kingmaker.

text.p: Once New Zealand's most popular politician, nationalist Winston Peters has seen his star wane since he began to forge workable policies from populist rhetoric.
But the charismatic Maori leader of the New Zealand First party still looks set to emerge as kingmaker after a general election on Saturday.

Peters, 51, says he wants to be prime minister. More realistically, he will be in a position to anoint either the ruling conservative National Party or the left-wing opposition led by the Labour Party.
Either party would need a coalition partner in order to govern, but Peters refuses to say which way he would sway.

He courts voters with promises of open, accountable government that puts ordinary New Zealanders' welfare above the interests of foreigners and big business. His party would limit foreign ownership of strategic assets to 24.9 percent.

"We think the resources of this country should be owned by the people of this country for the employment and wealth-creation and the benefit of this country," he said in a radio interview on Thursday.
Latest opinion polls show National averaging just under 33 percent support, with Labour on 26 percent, the left-wing Alliance on 15 and New Zealand First on 14.
Peters, a former National cabinet member, says Labour's economic policy "won't stack up", but has reserved his most vitriolic attacks for Prime Minister Jim Bolger.

Bolger sacked him as Maori Affairs Minister in 1991 and personal animosity between the two runs deep, but Peters on Thursday denied saying his party would only deal with National if Bolger was dumped as leader.
Of Scottish and Maori ancestry, Peters, a lawyer, trades on his personal charm and winning smile.

Accused by former colleagues of laziness when in cabinet, he has formidable stamina. He enjoys nightclubs (recently accompanied by bodyguards after unspecified threats), and survives on very little sleep. He is always immaculately dressed.

With a group of loyal supporters, Peters formed New Zealand First in 1993 after breaking with National. Its support peaked at 30 percent in February this year after Peters promised to cut immigration -- running at 55,000 a year -- "to the bone".

In a carefully worded speech, he referred to rows of "ostentatious houses" in an affluent Auckland suburb which is popular with Asian immigrants. He said immigration was pushing up house price inflation and interest rates, and the country of 3.5 million could not stand the strain.
Opponents were quick to label him racist, a charge which he denied. His popularity soared.
His style is reminiscent of his mentor, former National Prime Minister Sir Robert Muldoon, whose own brand of populism polarised New Zealand in the 1970s and early 1980s.
Muldoon's biographer, political scientist Barry Gustafson, has noted both could "articulate the concerns, resentments, frustrations of the ordinary people".

Allegations of conspiracies have been Peters' stock in trade. In 1994 he successfully led calls for an inquiry into allegations that top companies had evaded millions of dollars worth of tax through the Cook Islands tax haven.
